title: Can you structure these 12 public sector case questions in two minutes each?
description: 12 public sector case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes, as long as you start every one by defining what success means, because public sector prompts have no profit number to aim at. Once the objective is clear (fewer cars, more children fed, shorter waits), the structure follows: who is affected, what stands in the way, which levers work and what they cost. Here are 12 prompts: two minutes each, then open the model.
body:
How to use this set

Give yourself two minutes per prompt. Open with the objective and how you would measure it, then build three or four buckets. Most good public sector structures segment the people involved (who is affected, who is missing out), name the barriers, list the levers and finish with delivery: cost, politics and measurement. The model shows buckets, where to start and the trap. For the method, read what to ask first in a public sector case.

1. Should a city introduce a congestion charge?

Show a model structure
  • Objectives: less traffic, cleaner air or revenue; alternatives such as parking policy, bus lanes or a low-emission zone.
  • Impact: drivers, residents, businesses and public transport users; who gains and who loses.
  • Economics: set-up and running cost; revenue and what it pays for.
  • Implementation: public and political support; technology, enforcement and timing.

Where to start: objectives. The right charge depends on whether the goal is traffic, air quality or revenue.

The trap: running straight to revenue without asking what the city wants to achieve.

2. A government wants 1 million more women in work within five years.

Show a model structure
  • Who and where: which groups are out of work and why; regions and sectors with the biggest gap.
  • Barriers: childcare cost and availability; flexible hours, skills and transport.
  • Levers: childcare funding, tax and benefits; employer incentives and training.
  • Delivery: cost per extra woman in work; how to measure progress.

Where to start: who is out of work and why. The barriers differ by group. The target means about 200,000 a year for five years.

The trap: listing policies before segmenting who is out of work.

3. How would you increase organ donor registrations?

Show a model structure
  • Awareness: who knows they can register; campaigns and personal stories.
  • Ease: registering at moments people already fill in forms, such as driving licence applications, doctor visits or apps; opt-out laws change the default rather than active sign-ups.
  • Trust and family: fears and myths; families overruling a loved one's wishes.
  • Measurement: registrations versus actual donations; which channel converts best.

Where to start: ease. Defaults and convenient sign-up points tend to move registrations more than campaigns.

The trap: only proposing awareness campaigns.

4. A group of 20 schools has seen exam results fall for two years.

Show a model structure
  • Which schools and subjects: spread of the fall; which year groups.
  • Teachers: turnover, vacancies and supply staff; experience and training.
  • Students: attendance and intake changes; support for those falling behind.
  • Curriculum and leadership: curriculum or exam changes; school leaders and their priorities.

Where to start: which schools. A fall across all 20 and a fall in five need different answers.

The trap: assuming a group-wide cause before checking where the fall is.

5. A hospital's 30-day readmission rate is twice the national average.

Show a model structure
  • Which patients: condition, age and ward; planned versus emergency.
  • In hospital: treatment and early discharge; medication at discharge.
  • After discharge: follow-up appointments and community care; patients' understanding of their care.
  • Data: how readmissions are coded and counted; comparison with similar hospitals.

Where to start: which patients. Readmissions often cluster in a few conditions. Check the data too: a different counting method can make a hospital look worse than it is.

The trap: keeping everyone in longer, which is expensive and may not help.

6. Should a city council merge four small primary schools into two?

Show a model structure
  • Students and families: travel distance and places available; effect on results.
  • Costs: savings on buildings and staff; building works and transport.
  • Quality: teacher recruitment and class sizes; specialist teaching.
  • Community: support and opposition; use of the empty sites.

Where to start: students and families. The council will be judged on access and results.

The trap: treating it as a cost-saving exercise only.

7. How could a government help more women start businesses?

Show a model structure
  • Who and why not: barriers by sector and region; comparison with men starting businesses.
  • Money: access to loans and investors; grants and loan guarantees.
  • Skills and networks: mentoring and role models; accelerators.
  • Practical barriers: childcare and time; benefit and tax rules.

Where to start: who is not starting and why. Find the biggest barrier in each sector before choosing a lever.

The trap: running awareness campaigns only.

8. How can a city raise its household recycling rate from 35% to 50%?

Show a model structure
  • Collection: bins, frequency and food waste; flats versus houses.
  • Households: space for bins and convenience; incentives and rules.
  • Contamination: wrong items in bins; checks and feedback.
  • Processing: what local plants can sort; markets for recycled materials.

Where to start: collection. Adding food waste collection is often the biggest single lever, and flats usually lag houses.

The trap: running leaflet campaigns only.

9. How could a rural region double its tourism income in five years?

Show a model structure
  • More visitors: which markets and transport links; marketing and partnerships.
  • Longer stays: things to do and events; accommodation supply.
  • More spend: food, experiences and local products; higher-value visitors.
  • Seasons: off-season attractions; conferences and groups.

Where to start: longer stays. Overnight visitors spend far more per trip than day-trippers, on beds and meals. Doubling in five years needs about 15% growth a year.

The trap: chasing visitor numbers that bring traffic but little spend.

10. How could a council get more eligible children to take free school meals?

Show a model structure
  • Who is missing out: eligible but not registered; registered but not eating.
  • Registration: automatic enrolment using benefits data; simpler forms.
  • Take-up: quality and choice of food; stigma and payment systems.
  • Delivery: kitchen capacity and cost per meal; funding.

Where to start: automatic enrolment, which removes the paperwork barrier entirely.

The trap: improving menus while many eligible families never register.

11. How can a city's libraries double the number of people using them?

Show a model structure
  • Users and non-users: by age and area; why non-users stay away.
  • Offer: books and digital lending; events, study space and services.
  • Access: opening hours and locations; online and mobile.
  • Partnerships: schools, job centres and health services; community groups.

Where to start: who does not come and why. Target the biggest missing groups.

The trap: only buying more books.

12. How can a city get bus ridership back to pre-pandemic levels?

Show a model structure
  • Who stopped: commuters, students and older people; routes and times.
  • Service: frequency and reliability; bus lanes and journey times.
  • Price: fares, passes and daily caps; discounts for groups.
  • Perception: safety and cleanliness; information and apps.

Where to start: who stopped. Commuters now working from home need a different offer from older passengers who lost confidence.

The trap: cutting fares for everyone before knowing who stopped.

How to score your answer: find the people hidden by averages

Take the congestion charge. "Traffic falls" is not enough. A strong structure separates commuters who have a good public transport alternative, shift workers who start before the buses run, tradespeople carrying tools, local shops and residents. The fairness of the policy depends on these groups.

Money still matters, but carefully. An illustrative $10 charge paid by 50,000 vehicles each weekday raises $500,000 a day before exemptions, collection costs and enforcement. Yet if the charge works, fewer cars enter and revenue falls. Maximising revenue and reducing congestion can pull in opposite directions, which is exactly why you agree the objective first.

Check that your structure names a measurable outcome (journey times, air quality, access), a baseline to compare against, and who gains and who pays.

Where to practise next

Move on to 17 profitability prompts. For full public sector cases with data, try Riverside City or Kestrel Metro in the casebook, or keep drilling with the structuring drill.
